section.title: How Majestic Is Your Name
section.sectionRationale: A hymn of pure praise framed by a repeated refrain, moving from the majesty of God's name displayed in creation and even in infants' mouths, to wonder that this same God crowns frail humanity with glory and dominion over His creation.
section.thesis: The LORD's name is majestic in all the earth, His glory set above the heavens, yet this same God is mindful of small, mortal humanity, crowning them with glory and honor and placing all creation under their feet.
section.frameNote: A hymn framed by an opening and closing refrain (vv1, 9), moving through God's glory silencing the enemy through the mouths of infants (v2), wonder at the heavens and human smallness (vv3-4), and the crowning of humanity with dominion (vv5-8).

verses.text: O LORD, our Lord, how majestic is Your name in all the earth! You have set Your glory above the heavens.
From the mouths of children and infants You have ordained praise on account of Your adversaries, to silence the enemy and avenger.

units.label: What is man?
units.note: the son of man that You care for him

verses.text: When I behold Your heavens, the work of Your fingers, the moon and the stars, which You have set in place,
what is {{adam|man}} that You are mindful of him, or the {{benAdam|son of man}} that You care for him?
You made him a little lower than the angels; You crowned him with {{kavod|glory}} and honor.
You made him ruler of the works of Your hands; You have placed everything under his feet:
all sheep and oxen, and even the beasts of the field,
the birds of the air and the fish of the sea, all that swim the paths of the seas.
O LORD, our Lord, how majestic is Your name in all the earth!

adam.gloss: Man, humankind, the same word used for the first man in Genesis. Here it names the sheer wonder that the God whose glory towers over the heavens is mindful of humanity at all, small and mortal as we are.

benAdam.gloss: Son of man, a Hebrew phrase for a human being, emphasizing frailty and mortality. Jesus takes this phrase as His most common self-designation in the Gospels, and Hebrews 2:6-9 quotes this very verse of Christ, who was made lower than the angels and is now crowned with glory and honor.

kavod.gloss: Glory, honor, weight or substance, used both of God's own majesty, verse 1, and of the crown given to humanity, verse 5. Humanity's glory is derivative, a reflected honor granted by the God whose own glory is set above the heavens.

basic.context: Psalm 8 is a pure hymn of praise, framed by the same declaration at its start and end: how majestic is Your name in all the earth. Between the two refrains, David marvels that the God whose glory fills the heavens is mindful of small, mortal humanity, crowning them with glory and giving them dominion over the rest of creation.
basic.hermeneutics: This psalm meditates on Genesis 1's creation account, humanity made in God's image and given dominion, turning it into worship; the phrase 'son of man' here describes ordinary human frailty, but Hebrews 2 shows the New Testament reading this psalm as ultimately fulfilled in Jesus, the true and greater Son of Man.
basic.originalLanguages: David marvels that adam, humanity, and ben-adam, son of man, emphasizing frailty and smallness, are the object of God's mindful care. Humanity is crowned with kavod, glory or honor, the same weighty word used of God's own majesty in verse 1, a glory that is given, not inherent.
basic.typology: Humanity's original calling to have dominion over creation, though marred by the fall, anticipates Jesus, the true Son of Man, who alone fulfills this psalm completely, all things now placed under His feet, Hebrews 2:8-9.
basic.christ: Hebrews 2:6-9 quotes this psalm directly of Jesus: made lower than the angels for a little while, through His incarnation and suffering, and now crowned with glory and honor because He tasted death for everyone. What Adam forfeited, Christ, the last Adam, has secured for humanity forever.
basic.god: God is majestic beyond the heavens, yet His glory is displayed even in the simple praise of children, silencing His adversaries not with force but with the weakest human voices, showing that His power delights to work through apparent weakness.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis 1:26-28 gives humanity dominion over creation, the background this psalm celebrates. Matthew 21:16 quotes verse 2 of children praising Jesus in the temple. Hebrews 2:6-9 applies this whole psalm directly to Christ's incarnation, death, and exaltation.
basic.oneStory: Psalm 8 marvels that the majestic Creator crowns frail humanity with glory and dominion, a calling humanity forfeited in the fall but that Jesus, the true Son of Man, has fully recovered and secured, so that everything is indeed now, or will be, placed under His feet.

context.literary:
Psalm 8 is one long sentence of address. From the first verse to the last it speaks to God, 'You' and 'Your' again and again, and never talks about Him at a distance. The hymn is a piece of worship in the second person, and the reader is drawn into it as a fellow speaker.

The frame is the refrain of verses 1 and 9, with one small difference. Verse 9 repeats verse 1 but leaves out the line 'You have set Your glory above the heavens.' The outer edges of the psalm are the same words, and what lies between them is the explanation. The movement from the first refrain to the second is a movement from the God whose glory is beyond the heavens to the God whose name is majestic in all the earth. The psalm brings the glory down to earth in the course of its own singing.

The middle has a clear shape. Verses 2 to 4 pair the smallest and the largest things in view, infants and the whole sky, and then turn on the psalm's only question, 'what is man?' Everything after verse 4 is the answer. The answer is a string of verbs with God as the subject: 'You made him,' 'You crowned him,' 'You made him ruler,' 'You have placed.' Humanity does nothing in the answer; it receives.

The eye of the poet also moves. It begins above the heavens, looks up at moon and stars, and comes down through the list of creatures: sheep and oxen, the wild animals, the birds and finally the fish in the paths of the seas. That list runs opposite to the order of Genesis 1:26, where fish come first and livestock third. The psalm starts with the animals nearest to a shepherd and ends in the deep, so that the ruler's gaze descends. Only the moon and the stars are named, not the sun, and a reader can hear in that a psalm sung at night.
context.historical:
The heading assigns the psalm to David and directs it to the choirmaster 'according to Gittith.' The BSB notes that Gittith is probably a musical or liturgical term, and it appears again in the headings of Psalms 81 and 84. Its meaning is unknown, and the heading tells us only that the psalm belonged to the worship life of Israel.

David was a shepherd before he was a king, and the psalm has the feel of someone who has spent nights under the sky with sheep. It is not hard to imagine the origin of the question in verse 4 in a young man watching the stars from a hillside. The list of sheep first among the creatures in verse 7 fits that background, though the psalm does not claim it as autobiography.

The mention of the moon and stars carries weight for the first hearers. Israel's neighbors worshipped the lights of the sky, and Israel was warned not to be drawn into bowing down to the sun, the moon and the stars, Deuteronomy 4:19. Psalm 8 does the opposite of worship. It calls them 'the work of Your fingers' and things which God 'set in place.' The great lights are turned from gods into evidence of a Creator, as Genesis 1:16 does when it says God made the stars 'as well,' in a single phrase.

The claim that humanity wears a crown and rules would also have been striking. In the surrounding cultures the king was commonly the one pictured as the image and agent of the gods on earth. Genesis 1:26-27 gives the image to man and woman together, and Psalm 8 turns it into song. The vocation of ruling belongs to the human being as such, and the psalm invites every worshipper, not only the king, to marvel at it.

Verse 2 speaks of 'Your adversaries' and 'the enemy and avenger.' The psalm does not say who these are, and the first hearers would have known that Israel's enemies were numerous. The point is that they are silenced by praise from the smallest voices, and not by an army.
context.canonical:
Psalm 8 is one of the great psalms of creation, and it draws its vocabulary from Genesis 1. The 'dominion' of verse 6 answers Genesis 1:26-28, where God says man is to rule over the fish, the birds and the livestock. Genesis 2 shows what such rule looks like when it is exercised well, in the man's naming of the animals, Genesis 2:19-20, and in his charge to 'cultivate and keep' the garden, Genesis 2:15. Psalm 115:16 gives the same truth in a single line: 'The highest heavens belong to the LORD, but the earth He has given to mankind.'

The question of verse 4 is asked again elsewhere, and each time with a different tone. Psalm 144:3-4 asks the same words and answers, 'Man is like a breath; his days are like a passing shadow.' Job turns the question into a complaint: 'What is man that You should exalt him... and test him every moment?' Job 7:17-18. Job 25:6 calls man 'a maggot.' Psalm 8 is the version that answers with a crown. Psalm 103:15-16 and Psalm 90:3 supply the frailty that gives the psalm its wonder.

The New Testament uses the psalm four times. Jesus quotes verse 2 in the temple, Matthew 21:16. Paul quotes verse 6, 'God has put everything under His feet,' in 1 Corinthians 15:27, and again in Ephesians 1:22. Hebrews 2:6-9 quotes verses 4 to 6 in full. In each case the psalm is read as reaching its fulfillment in Christ, who is the man in whom the dominion is restored.

The psalm belongs beside Psalm 110:1, where the LORD says to David's Lord, 'Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet.' The feet of Psalm 8:6 and the footstool of Psalm 110 are joined in the apostolic preaching, and together they explain how the human dominion becomes the reign of the risen King.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
David wanted Israel to sing about their place in the world from below, from the ground where they stand, looking up at a sky they did not make. He meant them to feel the smallness of a human being and, in the same breath, the greatness of being noticed. The psalm is built to hold those two things in tension: wonder at how little we are, and wonder at how much we have been given.

He also meant to teach vocation. To be crowned is to be charged. The list of sheep, oxen, wild animals, birds and fish is a list of responsibilities. A human being is set over the works of God's hands as a steward, someone who answers to the Owner. That is why the psalm is a hymn to the name of the LORD and not a hymn to man. The glory is on loan.

The psalm was also a defense against two errors. One error says that humans are nothing, a mere accident under a vast sky, and the other says that they are the measure of everything. Psalm 8 answers both. We are small, yet mindful care rests on us, and we are crowned, yet what we wear is given. The refrain at the beginning and the end fixes the direction of the praise: the name of the LORD is majestic, and it is majestic in all the earth, which means in the places where humans live and work.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm describes what God has made of humanity, and it does not say that humanity has always done well with it. Read alone, verses 5 to 8 might sound like a triumphant report. The rest of the Bible tells us that the rule has been abused, that the ground was cursed, and that creation was 'subjected to futility,' Romans 8:20. Hebrews 2:8 says plainly, 'at present we do not see everything subject to him.' So the psalm records a calling and a gift, not a completed achievement.

What follows for us is a way of living. Dominion, as Genesis 2:15 shows, is a form of service, cultivating and keeping. A person who has read Psalm 8 rightly does not treat animals or the land as things to be used up, since they are 'the works of Your hands' and belong to the LORD. Nor does he treat other people as animals to be ruled. The rule of the psalm is over creatures, and not over other humans.

Verse 2 gives an example of a different kind. The psalm does not tell parents to stage the praise of children, and it does not say that all children's speech is holy. It says that God has ordained praise from mouths that the world does not count, and it is Jesus who shows what that looks like in Matthew 21:16. The prescription for the reader is to keep the door open for such voices, and not to be like the chief priests, who were indignant.

debates.question: Who are the beings the human is made 'a little lower than'?

views.label: Angels
views.case: The Septuagint translates the Hebrew word here as 'angels,' and Hebrews 2:7 follows it. The BSB likewise reads 'angels.' On this view humanity stands just beneath the heavenly court in dignity.

views.label: God Himself
views.case: The Hebrew word is elohim, the ordinary word for God, and a footnote in the BSB offers 'than God.' Read this way, the human is made almost like God, which suits the way the verse continues with glory and honor, words used of God's own majesty, and the echo of the image of God in Genesis 1:26-27.

views.label: The heavenly beings or the divine council
views.case: Another footnote offers 'the heavenly beings.' The word elohim can name the members of God's court, as in Psalm 82:1, and the psalm may mean that humanity stands just below that company.

debates.bearing: All three views keep the main point: the human being is placed very high, yet beneath God. Hebrews is not troubled by the difference, since it uses the Greek text to show that the Son took a lower place for a time in order to be crowned.

debates.question: Is Psalm 8 about humanity in general or about the Messiah?

views.label: It is about humanity, later fulfilled in Christ
views.case: The psalm's question, 'what is man?', is about the human race, and its language follows Genesis 1:26-28. Hebrews reads it as being fulfilled in the one true man, Jesus, because humanity as a whole has not yet reached the promised rule, Hebrews 2:8-9.

views.label: It is a direct prophecy of the Messiah
views.case: Some read the psalm as speaking of the Son of Man from the outset, especially since the title has a messianic sense in Daniel 7:13-14. On this view the psalm is a single line of promise that runs straight to Jesus.

views.label: It has a double reference
views.case: Others say the psalm has two layers: it praises the ordinary dignity of every human being and, in the same words, looks ahead to the one who would perfectly fulfill that role. Paul's use of it in 1 Corinthians 15:27 and Ephesians 1:22 fits this pattern.

debates.bearing: The first and third views honor the plain sense of the psalm, and the New Testament honors the same sense by showing where human dignity reaches its goal. What is said of humanity is true of Christ first, and of us in Him.

debates.question: What does it mean that praise is ordained 'from the mouths of children and infants'?

views.label: Literal children and babies, as a sign of God's power in weakness
views.case: The verse names children and nursing infants, the weakest voices, and says that God builds strength on them. Paul later says that God chose the weak things of the world to shame the strong, 1 Corinthians 1:27.

views.label: The lowly and the childlike among God's people
views.case: Some read the children as a figure for those who receive God's revelation with simple trust. Jesus praises the Father for hiding things from the wise and revealing them to little children, Matthew 11:25, and says that the humble are the greatest in the kingdom, Matthew 18:4.

views.label: Jesus' own use in the temple
views.case: When the children cry 'Hosanna to the Son of David,' Jesus quotes the verse as fulfilled, Matthew 21:15-16. On this view the verse is given its clearest sense by what happens when the Messiah arrives in the temple.

debates.bearing: The views agree that God's power is not measured by human strength. Whichever sense is stressed, the answer to the enemy is made by those with no worldly force.

study.originalLanguages:
The two words for 'man' in verse 4 are not the same. The first line asks 'what is enosh,' a word for a frail, mortal human being, and the second line asks about ben adam, the son of Adam. The first word is used elsewhere to stress weakness. Psalm 90:3 says God returns 'man' to dust, Psalm 103:15 says 'As for man, his days are like grass,' and Job 25:6 calls him a maggot. Job 7:17 twists the question of Psalm 8 into an accusation, asking why God should take so much notice of such a creature. The wonder of Psalm 8 depends on how weak the word makes us.

The two verbs of divine attention are zakar and paqad. The first is to remember, to be mindful, and it is the word for God's remembering in covenant. The second is to visit or attend to. It is the verb used when 'the LORD attended to Sarah as He had said,' Genesis 21:1. God does not merely think about humanity; He comes to them and acts. The BSB's 'care for him' is a good paraphrase.

Verse 5 turns on a pair of verbs. 'You made him a little lower' is a verb that means to cause to lack, so the phrase can be heard as 'You made him lack a little of.' Then, 'You crowned him,' from a verb for encircling and crowning. The crown is glory and honor, kavod and hadar, the second word being splendor or majesty. The phrase 'a little' can be read as a small degree or a short time. Hebrews takes the second sense, since the Greek word it uses can mean either, and so it applies the psalm to Jesus' brief time below.

The word for ruling in verse 6 is mashal, and the verb in Genesis 1:26 is radah. Both mean to rule, and the psalm restates the vocation of Genesis in a fresh word. The phrase 'under his feet' is a symbol of conquered enemies elsewhere, Psalm 110:1, and here it stands for authority over creation.

In verse 2, the Hebrew says God has 'founded strength' from the mouths of children and infants, the latter being nursing babies. The Greek translation renders the word for strength as praise, and it is this form that Jesus quotes in Matthew 21:16. The BSB footnote records both. The Septuagint's reading makes explicit what the Hebrew leaves as an image: the strength that God builds is the strength of worship.

The second half of verse 1 is a hard line. The verb form in 'You have set Your glory' is unusual, and translators have wrestled with it. Whatever the exact grammar, the sense of the glory placed above the heavens is not in doubt. The address 'O LORD, our Lord' joins the name YHWH to adonenu, so that the covenant name and the title of master stand side by side and the psalm is spoken by the people in the plural, 'our.'

typology.fulfillment: The first human pair were made to rule the works of God's hands, and they failed, so the crown lay in the dust. Hebrews takes the psalm and says, 'we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, now crowned with glory and honor because He suffered death,' Hebrews 2:9. Paul reads the last Adam in the same way, 1 Corinthians 15:45. The correspondence is between the first man and the last, and the escalation is that the second Man wins the crown by obedience and by the cross, and gives it to others. The type falls short in that Adam's rule was over creatures only, while Christ's rule extends over every power, Ephesians 1:21-22.

typology.type: The praise of children in the temple, Psalm 8:2
typology.fulfillment: God builds His strength out of voices no one counts. The pattern is fulfilled when, in the temple courts, children shout 'Hosanna to the Son of David,' and Jesus answers the indignant priests with the words of verse 2, Matthew 21:15-16. The escalation is that the praise the psalm gives to the LORD is now given to Jesus, and He accepts it. The type falls short because the psalm speaks of a general pattern, while Matthew shows a single moment in which it is filled with a name.

The order of the verse, a little lower, then crowned, becomes the shape of the gospel. Paul writes that Christ, existing in the form of God, 'emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant,' and that therefore God 'exalted Him to the highest place,' Philippians 2:6-11. Hebrews says he was made perfect through suffering, Hebrews 2:10. The correspondence is real, but the psalm sees a status given to all humanity, while the New Testament sees a descent that is unique to the Son and an ascent that brings many with Him.

typology.type: Dominion shared with the redeemed, Psalm 8:6
typology.fulfillment: The rule of humanity is not lost for good. Those redeemed by the Lamb are made 'a kingdom and priests to serve our God, and they will reign upon the earth,' Revelation 5:9-10, and are 'co-heirs with Christ,' Romans 8:17. The correspondence is that the vocation of Genesis is restored. The type is surpassed because the rule of the redeemed comes through the death of another and is exercised in a renewed creation, not the present one, Hebrews 2:5.

study.christ:
Hebrews 2 is the key that opens the psalm to Christ, and its argument runs in steps. The writer begins by saying that the world to come has not been put under angels, Hebrews 2:5, and then quotes Psalm 8:4 to 6 as a witness. He notes a problem: God 'left nothing outside of his control,' yet 'at present we do not see everything subject to him,' Hebrews 2:8. The psalm speaks of dominion, and the world shows no such thing. Then comes the turn: 'But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, now crowned with glory and honor because He suffered death,' Hebrews 2:9. The one man in whom the psalm is fulfilled is Jesus, and He gets there by way of the cross.

The step matters for how we read the phrase 'a little lower.' Hebrews hears it as a short time below, the days of the incarnation, and so the psalm becomes a description of the path of the Son. He goes down into flesh and blood, Hebrews 2:14, He is made like His brothers in every way, Hebrews 2:17, and He tastes death for everyone. Then He is crowned. The pattern is the same as in Philippians 2:6-11, where the Son who emptied Himself is exalted and given the name above all names.

Paul uses the last line of the psalm the other way round, looking at the crowned Man on the throne. When God raised Christ and seated Him at His right hand, 'God put everything under His feet and made Him head over everything for the church,' Ephesians 1:22. In 1 Corinthians 15:27 the same verse explains the sequence of Christ's reign until the last enemy, death, is destroyed. Psalm 110:1 stands behind both texts.

The psalm also leads to Christ by the title 'son of man.' In the Gospels it is Jesus' favorite name for Himself. Sometimes it points to the glory of Daniel 7:13-14, where One like a son of man receives an everlasting dominion, and sometimes to service, 'the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many,' Mark 10:45. Psalm 8 holds both ideas together. The son of man is the frail creature, and he is also the one crowned to rule.

Jesus does more than fulfill the psalm; He speaks it. In the temple He quotes verse 2 and receives the praise of children that the psalm gives to the LORD. Only someone who stood in the place of God could take the words that way.

The link should be drawn with care. Psalm 8 is first about humanity, and the New Testament does not erase that sense. What it does is to show the whole human story moving toward one man. Christ is the true Man, 'the image of the invisible God,' Colossians 1:15, and those united with Him are being 'conformed to the image of His Son,' Romans 8:29. He is the one in whom we recover the crown.
study.god:
The psalm shows a God who is enormously great and remarkably attentive. His glory is set above the heavens, verse 1, and yet the stars are 'the work of Your fingers,' verse 3. The word fingers is the language of a craftsman working with delicate skill. There is no strain in it. The one who made the sky as an artist makes a small piece is the one who, in Isaiah 40:26, calls every star by name and misses none.

He is a God who condescends. The psalm's central question, 'what is man that You are mindful of him?', assumes that God has every reason to overlook us. The reason He does not is nowhere given in the psalm except in His own character. Scripture never explains God's care by our worth; it points to His own decision. Psalm 115:1 says, 'Not to us, O LORD, not to us, but to Your name be the glory.' It is grace, and grace is the kind of thing that is only ever explained by the giver.

He is a God who shares. The Creator crowns a creature with glory and gives him rule. That the Lord of the universe delegates authority to something so small is one of the strange things the Bible says about Him. He is not threatened by giving; His own glory is not lessened when He crowns another, and He remains 'our Lord.' The crown is real, and it is given.

He is a God who works by weakness. He builds strength out of the mouths of infants to silence the enemy, verse 2. Paul draws the same lesson: God chose the weak things of the world to shame the strong, 1 Corinthians 1:27. The scandal is intended. It ensures that no one can claim the victory for himself.

He is a God with a name. The refrain speaks of 'Your name' and calls Him both LORD and Lord. The name is the revealed character of God, and it is 'majestic in all the earth,' which means that His greatness is not confined to the temple or the heavens. Psalm 148:13 says His splendor is above the earth and the heavens.

For worship, the psalm teaches us to stand in the right place. We are not gods, and we are not nothing. Under the night sky the right response is not to shrink into despair or to swell with pride but to sing, and to sing with the exact words with which the song began. The circle of the refrain tells us that the end of wonder is not an answer but a doxology.

crossReferences.note: The background of the whole psalm. God makes man in His image to rule over fish, birds and livestock, and blesses them. Psalm 8:5-8 is a meditation on that text, singing it back to God as wonder. The list of creatures is the same, though the order is reversed.

The man is placed in the garden 'to cultivate and keep it.' It shows what dominion looks like in practice, as service to what is entrusted. It guards the reading of Psalm 8:6 against any idea that being ruler means being a tyrant.

Job asks, 'What is man that You should exalt him?' and turns the wonder of Psalm 8:4 into a complaint that God pays him too much attention. The two texts use nearly the same words for opposite moods, and they show that the same fact can be a comfort or a burden.

David asks, 'O LORD, what is man, that You regard him?' and answers, 'Man is like a breath.' It gives the other half of the picture, human frailty. Read with Psalm 8, it shows that the crown is put on a head that is as brief as a shadow.

'The heavens declare the glory of God.' Psalm 19 and Psalm 8 both start with the sky, but Psalm 19 lets the skies speak to us, while Psalm 8 turns to speak back to the God who made them. Together they give the two directions of creation's praise.

'Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet.' The feet of Psalm 8:6 and the footstool of Psalm 110 are joined in the New Testament, so that the human dominion is understood as the reign of the enthroned Christ.

The children cry 'Hosanna to the Son of David,' and Jesus quotes Psalm 8:2 to the indignant priests. He takes the ordained praise of the psalm to describe what is happening around Himself, and shows that the weakest voices may see what the leaders do not.

Paul quotes 'God has put everything under His feet' and applies it to Christ. The verse shows the order in which the dominion of Psalm 8:6 is realized, through the resurrection and the reign of the Son until death itself is destroyed.

The fullest New Testament reading of Psalm 8. The writer quotes verses 4 to 6, admits that we do not yet see everything subject to man, and then says 'we see Jesus.' The psalm is read as the path of the Son, from below the angels to the crown.

God raised Christ, seated Him far above all rule and authority, and 'put everything under His feet.' The passage picks up Psalm 8:6 to describe the exaltation of Christ, and adds that He is head over everything 'for the church,' so that the dominion is shared.

Creation waits for the sons of God, having been 'subjected to futility.' It is the rest of the story after Psalm 8: the rule given to humanity was damaged, and creation groans until the children of God are revealed and the bondage to decay is lifted.

The redeemed are made 'a kingdom and priests to serve our God, and they will reign upon the earth.' It answers Psalm 8:6 in the last book of the Bible and shows the dominion given back, through the Lamb, to people from every tribe and nation.

study.oneStory:
Psalm 8 goes back to the sixth day. The God who made everything and called it good made man and woman in His image and told them to rule, Genesis 1:26-28. The psalm is a meditation on that scene as it looks from the ground, at night, from someone who knows how small the creature is. It shows what the human calling was meant to feel like: astonishment and gratitude, not entitlement.

The story then breaks. Adam and Eve reached for a different kind of glory in the garden, Genesis 3, and the rule they were given turned into toil, thorns and death. Paul says that through one man sin and death entered the world, Romans 5:12, and that creation was subjected to futility, Romans 8:20. The animals of the psalm's list, the ground and the sea were affected by the failure of their ruler. Job speaks for many when he takes the question of the psalm and turns it bitter, Job 7:17-18.

Yet the crown is not taken back. God's purposes for humanity stand, and the rest of the Old Testament keeps them alive: in the blessing to Abraham, in the kings of Israel, and in the hope of a Son of Man who would receive everlasting dominion, Daniel 7:13-14. David, who wrote the psalm, was a king who ruled and failed, and so pointed beyond himself.

The story turns in Jesus, who takes the lower place, is crowned for suffering death and is given all things, Hebrews 2:9, Ephesians 1:22. The children shout in the temple, Matthew 21:16, and the enemy is silenced, not by force, but by a cross and an empty tomb. Now we live in the gap that Hebrews describes, where we do not yet see everything subject to man but do see Jesus. The church prays and serves in that gap, as those who share His life and will share His rule, Romans 8:17.

The story ends in a world where the psalm is at last true. Those redeemed by the Lamb 'will reign upon the earth,' Revelation 5:10, and the creation, set free from its bondage to decay, enters the glorious freedom of the children of God, Romans 8:21. The servants of God 'will reign forever and ever,' Revelation 22:5, and every creature in heaven and on earth and in the sea joins in praise, Revelation 5:13. The refrain of Psalm 8 is the shape of that final chorus. In the new creation, the name of the LORD is majestic in all the earth, and the crowned creature bows down and sings.

sermon.title: How Majestic Is Your Name
sermon.why: Begg examines Psalm 8's right reflection on both God and man, urging big thoughts of the Creator and small thoughts of ourselves, and shows how seeing God and our sins rightly leads us to be reconciled to Him through Christ.

quiz.q: What is the refrain that opens and closes Psalm 8?

options.text: O LORD, our Lord, how majestic is Your name in all the earth.
options.note: This exact declaration frames the whole psalm as an inclusio.

options.text: The heavens declare the glory of God.
options.note: This is the opening line of Psalm 19, a related but different psalm.

options.text: Blessed is the man who fears the LORD.
options.note: This phrase belongs to other psalms, such as Psalm 112, not Psalm 8.

options.text: The psalm has no refrain.
options.note: Verses 1 and 9 are identical, forming a clear refrain.

quiz.q: How does God silence the enemy and avenger, according to verse 2?

options.text: Through the praise from the mouths of children and infants.
options.note: This surprising image shows God's power displayed through the weakest human voices.

options.text: Through the might of Israel's armies.
options.note: The verse specifically credits the praise of infants and children, not military force.

options.text: Through natural disasters.
options.note: No natural disaster is mentioned; the specific means named is the praise of children.

options.text: The psalm does not explain how the enemy is silenced.
options.note: Verse 2 explicitly names the praise of children and infants as the means.

quiz.q: What does the psalmist marvel at in verses 3-4?

options.text: That God, whose heavens are the work of His fingers, is mindful of and cares for small, mortal humanity.
options.note: This is the psalm's central wonder, the contrast between cosmic vastness and personal care.

options.text: That the stars are more numerous than he expected.
options.note: The wonder is specifically about God's care for humanity in light of the heavens' vastness, not merely counting stars.

options.text: That humanity has built impressive cities.
options.note: Human achievement is not the psalm's focus; God's care despite human smallness is.

options.text: Nothing in particular; these verses are purely descriptive.
options.note: Verses 3-4 pose a direct, wondering question about God's mindfulness of humanity.

quiz.q: What has God given to humanity, according to verses 5-8?

options.text: Glory and honor, and dominion over the works of His hands, including all animals, birds, and fish.
options.note: This is the psalm's description of humanity's God-given dignity and rule, echoing Genesis 1.

options.text: Immortality and freedom from all suffering.
options.note: The psalm describes dominion and glory, not a promise of immortality or freedom from suffering.

options.text: Wealth and political power over other nations.
options.note: The dominion described is over creation, animals and creatures, not political rule over nations.

options.text: Nothing; humanity is left with no special role.
options.note: Verses 5-8 explicitly describe a significant, God-given role of dominion and honor.

quiz.q: How does Hebrews 2:6-9 use this psalm?

options.text: It applies the psalm directly to Jesus, made lower than the angels for a little while and now crowned with glory and honor because He tasted death for everyone.
options.note: This is a direct New Testament application of Psalm 8 to Christ's incarnation and exaltation.

options.text: It rejects Psalm 8 as no longer applicable after Christ's coming.
options.note: Hebrews 2 embraces and fulfills Psalm 8's language in Christ, rather than rejecting it.

options.text: It applies Psalm 8 only to angels, not to humanity or Christ.
options.note: Hebrews 2 specifically contrasts Christ's temporary lowering beneath the angels with His subsequent exaltation, applying the psalm to Him, not to angels.

options.text: It has no connection to Psalm 8 at all.
options.note: Hebrews 2:6-8 directly quotes Psalm 8:4-6 and applies it to Christ.

questions: The psalm moves from the vastness of God's glory to wonder at His care for small, mortal humanity. Where in your life do you need to be reminded that God's greatness does not make Him distant or indifferent to you personally?

God silences His adversaries through the praise of children and infants, not through displays of raw power. Where might God be using something small or seemingly weak in your life to accomplish something significant?

Humanity's glory and dominion are described as given by God, not earned or inherent. How does remembering that your dignity comes from God's gift, not your own achievement, change the way you view your worth or your work?

Jesus is the true Son of Man who fulfills this psalm completely, with all things ultimately placed under His feet. How does trusting that Christ's reign is secure change the way you face situations that currently feel out of control?

The psalm begins and ends with the same declaration of God's majestic name. What would it look like for your own days this week to begin and end with genuine wonder at who God is, rather than being framed only by your own tasks and worries?

translationNotes.note: Upon the Gittith likely names a musical instrument or tune associated with Gath, appearing in the superscriptions of three psalms, 8, 81, and 84, though its exact meaning is uncertain.

A little lower than the angels renders Elohim, which can mean God, gods, or heavenly beings; the Septuagint and Hebrews 2:7 both render it angels, the traditional and most widely followed translation.

Son of man, ben-adam, is a common Hebrew idiom for a human being, emphasizing mortality and frailty; Jesus later adopts 'Son of Man' as His most frequent self-designation in the Gospels, drawing on both this psalm and Daniel 7:13-14.
